title: Why did African buyers decide what Manchester made?
teaches: West Africa's own textile industries; cloth currencies; buyers who made Gujarati and Manchester producers match local patterns; cloth as the largest good traded for enslaved people; the Atlantic markets behind British cotton

blocks.text: Among the papers of English slave traders in the 1750s are lists of the goods a ship carried to the West African coast. One, for a voyage to the Windward Coast in 1756, lists goods worth £2,418 to buy 250 people.[^cargo] Most of the value is cloth. Some of it is Indian, cottons with names such as *niccanees*, a striped cloth from Gujarat. Some of it is English, made in Manchester and named to match: Manchester niccanees, made to imitate the Indian ones.

Lists like this are records of the Atlantic slave trade, in which about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships between the 16th and 19th centuries and about 10.7 million survived the crossing to the Americas.[^voyages] They also show something about how that trade worked. The African merchants and rulers who sold captives to European ships would accept only certain goods, and among those goods cloth came first. In this lesson we look at why: what West Africa already made, what its buyers wanted, and how their demands shaped the British cotton industry.

West Africa had large textile industries of its own. Cotton was grown across the savanna from Senegal to Lake Chad. Men wove on narrow treadle looms that made long strips, often only 10 to 20 cm wide, which were then sewn edge to edge into a cloth; in many areas women wove wider cloth on upright looms. The city of Kano, in what is now northern Nigeria, was famous for its indigo dye pits, and the German traveller Heinrich Barth wrote in the 1850s that Kano's dyed cloth was worn from the Atlantic coast to the Sahara. Yoruba weavers made *aso oke*, and Asante weavers in what is now Ghana made the patterned strip cloth later known as kente, using silk unravelled from imported cloth for the brightest colours.

In several regions cloth worked as money. Standard strips or pieces of cotton were used to pay taxes, set prices and settle debts, from the Senegal valley to the Lake Chad basin. A people with their own cloth and their own cloth money were not buyers who would take anything offered. Imported cloth had to compete with local cloth, and it sold only if it offered something local weavers did not: a colour, a pattern, a fineness, or simply a large quantity quickly.

European traders on the coast complained constantly in their letters that African buyers were particular. A stripe had to be the right width and colour; a check had to have the right number of threads; a piece had to be the right length; a cloth that had sold well one year might be refused the next because tastes had changed. Different stretches of the coast wanted different cloths. Goods that did not match came back unsold, and a ship that could not sell its cargo stayed on the coast longer, losing money and losing crew and captives to disease.

The cloths African buyers wanted most in the 17th and 18th centuries were Indian: checks, stripes and plain blue cottons from Gujarat and the Coromandel coast. British and Dutch companies bought them in India, shipped them to Europe, and re-exported them to Africa. For British traders in the 18th century, textiles were usually the largest single category of goods exchanged for captives, often more than half of a cargo's value, and Indian cloth was a large share of the textiles.

blocks.caption: Cloth in the 18th-century Atlantic and Indian Ocean trades. Indian cloth and Manchester imitations went to West Africa; captives were taken to the Americas; sugar, and later raw cotton, came to Britain.

blocks.text: The same was true on the other side of Africa. On the East African coast, Gujarati merchants sold Indian cloth for ivory, gold and later cloves, and they adapted designs to local taste. In the 19th century, buyers in Zanzibar and the interior preferred a heavy unbleached American cotton sheeting, which they called *merikani*, to the British cloth that was cheaper. Here too, the buyer decided.

Indian cloth was not always available. Wars in Europe interrupted shipping, the East India Company's supplies varied from year to year, and after 1721 printed Indian cloth could not be sold in Britain at all, only re-exported. Manchester and the towns around it began to make cloths for the African trade, at first of linen and cotton, imitating Indian checks and stripes and giving them the Indian names. Traders sent samples from the coast back to Manchester so that the copies would match what African buyers accepted. When a war cut off Indian supply, Manchester's share of the trade jumped.

The economic historian Joseph Inikori has argued that these Atlantic markets, in Africa and in the plantation colonies of the Americas, were essential to the growth of the British cotton industry: they were large, they grew fast, and they demanded cheap cloth of consistent quality in large quantities, which favoured machine production. Other historians give more weight to the home market and to technical change in Britain. Lesson 17 returns to the wider debate about slavery and British industry.

Cloth was the main currency of a trade in human beings. The demand of African buyers for particular cloths decided what weavers in Gujarat and Lancashire made; the captives bought with that cloth were carried to plantations that, within a few decades, would grow the raw cotton for Lancashire's mills. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807, but the cotton trade built partly on it went on growing.

blocks.caption: Five questions on cloth and Africa.

items.ask: West Africa already made plenty of cotton cloth. Why did imported cloth sell at all?
choices: It offered particular colours, patterns or quantities that local weavers did not supply
African weavers had stopped weaving
Imported cloth was always cheaper
Local cloth was banned by African rulers
items.why: Imported cloth competed with a strong local industry, so it sold only when it gave buyers something different, which is why buyers were so particular.

items.ask: A slave ship arrives with checks in the wrong colours. What is likely to happen?
choices: The cloth is refused, and the ship stays on the coast longer at great cost
The buyers accept it at a discount
The captain dyes it on board
Nothing; any cloth was accepted
items.why: African merchants specified what they would accept. Unsold cargo meant longer stays on the coast, with deaths among crew and captives and lost money.

items.ask: Why did Manchester weavers give their cloths Indian names such as niccanees?
choices: They were copying Indian cloths that African buyers already knew and wanted
The cloth was made in India
The names were Lancashire words
To avoid the Calico Acts
items.why: The names signalled to buyers that the copy matched the Indian original they trusted.

items.ask: In 19th-century Zanzibar, buyers preferred American sheeting to cheaper British cloth. What does that show?
choices: Buyers chose by quality and taste, not only by price
British cloth could not reach Zanzibar
American cloth was made in Africa
Zanzibar banned British goods
items.why: Merikani was heavier and wore better. As in West Africa, buyers set the terms that producers had to meet.

items.ask: What is Joseph Inikori's argument about Atlantic markets and British cotton?
choices: Fast-growing African and colonial demand for cheap, uniform cloth pushed British cotton towards mass production
Africa supplied Britain's raw cotton in the 18th century
The slave trade had no connection to cotton
British cotton grew only because of home demand
items.why: Inikori stresses the size and growth of Atlantic markets. Other historians weigh home demand and technology more heavily, which lesson 17 takes up.

summary: **Cloth bought captives.** In the 18th-century British slave trade, textiles were usually the largest category of goods exchanged for people.
**West Africa had its own cloth industries.** Strip looms, Kano's indigo pits, Yoruba and Asante weaving, and cloth used as money.
**So imported cloth had to compete.** It sold only when it offered colours, patterns or quantities local weavers did not.
**Buyers set the terms.** African merchants specified stripes, checks, lengths and colours, and refused goods that did not match.
**Indian cloth came first.** Gujarati and Coromandel cottons were re-exported from Europe to West Africa and sold directly in East Africa.
**Manchester copied India.** Lancashire made imitations with Indian names, and gained share when wars cut Indian supply.
**Atlantic markets fed British cotton.** Inikori argues their growth pushed British production towards cheap, uniform cloth; others stress home demand.
**The trades were linked.** Cloth bought captives, and captives grew the cotton that later fed Lancashire.

cargo.title: The 1756 list
cargo.text: The list is one of many such abstracts used by historians of the trade, including Joseph Inikori. Cargo lists recorded what was carried out, not what was finally exchanged, and prices on the coast changed with supply and demand.

voyages.title: Where the numbers come from
voyages.text: The figures are estimates from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (slavevoyages.org), built from records of about 36,000 voyages, for the years 1501 to 1866.
